title: Comparative well-being of the self-employed and paid employees in the USA
abstract: Drawing upon the job demand-control model and analyzing more than 600,000 responses from the nationally representative Gallup survey data over the 2010–2016 period, we find that self-employed individuals in the USA report lower life satisfaction than paid employees (i.e., evaluative well-being). The self-employed also experience both positive feelings such as happiness and enjoyment and negative feelings such as anger and stress more than their wage-earning peers, leading to a stark emotional dichotomy in how they experience their daily lives (i.e., hedonic well-being) consistent with both high job control and high job demand that are prevalent in self-employment. Lastly, the self-employed also report more health problems and lower physical well-being. Income (and low local unemployment to some extent) successfully mitigates the negative effects of self-employment on subjective well-being while enhancing the positive, but education does not do so. Overall, the results suggest that self-employment is associated with predominantly negative well-being effects in the USA.
summary_en: Are self-employed people happier than wage-earners? Bencsik and Chuluun analyse 600,000+ responses from US Gallup data 2010-2016 using the job demand-control model. They find self-employed Americans report LOWER overall life satisfaction than paid employees, but experience both more positive emotions (happiness, enjoyment) and more negative emotions (anger, stress) — an emotional dichotomy consistent with high job control + high job demand. They also report more health problems and lower physical well-being. Income (and low local unemployment) mitigates the negative well-being effects, but education does not.
data_used: Gallup-Healthways Well-Being Index daily survey data 2010-2016 covering 600,000+ US respondents, with self-employment status, life satisfaction, hedonic well-being, and health measures.
policy_relevance: Hungarian small-business and self-employment policy at IFKA, MFB, and Pénzügyminisztérium. The paper shows self-employment is associated with mixed well-being outcomes: economic income partly compensates for the well-being costs. Useful framework for designing Hungarian SME-support programmes that target both income and well-being outcomes.
